# Epistle of Barnabas — Chapter 4 (SOPHIA Consensus)

**Source:** Codex Sinaiticus, Epistle of Barnabas 4
**Agent:** SOPHIA (Consensus)
**Date:** 2026-03-17

---

## Consensus Translation

1. Let us therefore investigate the present state of affairs and search out what is able to save us. Let us flee from every sort of lawlessness entirely, lest the deeds of lawlessness gain mastery over us; and let us hate the error of the present age, so that we may be loved in the age that is to come.
2. Let us give no permission to our soul to consort with the sinners and the lawless, lest we become like them.
3. The great stumbling-block is at hand, of which it has been written — as Enoch says: "For to this end the Master has cut short the times and the days, so that his Beloved might hasten and come to his inheritance."
4. And the prophet also speaks thus: "Ten kingdoms shall reign upon the earth, and after them there shall arise a small king, and he shall humble three of the kings together."
5. Likewise Daniel speaks of the same: "And I saw the fourth beast, wicked and strong and more savage than all the beasts of the earth, and how there arose ten horns out of it, and from among them a small horn, and how it humiliated three of the great horns together."
6. You ought therefore to understand. And I further ask you this — being as I am one of your number, and loving each of you more than my own soul: pay attention to yourselves now and do not be made like some who heap up your sins and say that the covenant is both theirs and ours.
7. Ours it is; but they lost it forever in this way: when Moses had already received it. For the scripture says: "And Moses was on the mountain fasting forty days and forty nights, and he received the covenant from the Lord — tablets of stone written by the finger of the hand of the Lord."
8. But they turned to idols and lost it. For the Lord says thus: "Moses, Moses, come down quickly, for your people whom you brought out of the land of Egypt have acted lawlessly." And Moses understood, and threw the two tablets from his hands; and their covenant was shattered — so that the covenant of Jesus the Beloved might be sealed in our hearts in hope of his faith.
9. But wishing to write many things — not as a teacher but as befits a friend who loves you, omitting nothing of what we possess — I have been earnest in writing to you, being a poor slave. Yet let us give heed in this last time.
10. For the whole time of our faith will profit us nothing if we do not resist now, in this lawless time and against the coming stumbling-blocks, as befits sons of God.
11. So that the Black One may find no means of entry, let us flee every vanity, let us utterly hate the works of the evil way. Do not withdraw into yourself, do not live in isolation as though you were already justified, but come together in the same place and discuss the common good.
12. For the scripture says: "Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes and discerning in their own sight!" Let us become spiritual; let us become a perfect temple for God. To the extent that is in us, let us meditate on the fear of God and strive to keep his commandments, that we may be glad in his righteous judgments.

---

## Council Notes

- vv.3-5: Key apocalyptic section. Barnabas cites Daniel 7 (the four beasts, the ten horns, the small horn) and applies it to Rome — the "fourth beast" = Rome, the "small king" = likely Vespasian or Domitian. This is one of the earliest Christian interpretations of Daniel's four-kingdom schema as Rome. Combined with the Enoch citation, this places the letter in an apocalyptic register despite its otherwise didactic tone.
- v.6: "The covenant is both theirs and ours" — this is the position Barnabas explicitly rejects. He represents Jews and Christians as having made this claim; he counters that the covenant belongs solely to Christians because Israel forfeit it through idolatry at Sinai.
- v.8: "The covenant of Jesus the Beloved" — Barnabas reads the Sinai narrative as prefiguring the transfer of the covenant from Israel to the church.
- v.11: "The Black One" (*ho melas*) — a personification of evil/the devil unusual in early Christian literature; may reflect an Egyptian or Jewish background.
- v.11: "Do not live in isolation as though you were already justified" — an anti-individualist, anti-perfectionist warning; probably aimed at proto-gnostic or pneumatic circles.
